title: Stop Telling Agents How — Dan Barrett, Raymond Weitekamp & Jose Montes de Oca, OpenProse
talk_summary: OpenProse is a markdown-based declarative 'contract' language for event-driven multi-agent workflows, compiled by whatever coding-agent harness you already use. The core claim is that declaring outcomes (not procedures) lets any harness self-shape, and that fresh sessions benchmarked against a written contract beat self-review loops.

takeaways.technique: Fresh-session adversarial review against a written contract
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of letting the building agent self-check (which is biased to think it did well), they spawn new review sessions that are benchmarked against a declarative contract, and the builder cannot mark its job complete until reviewer feedback is addressed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you don't want the same model checking the thing that was done. So, you're spawning new sessions and and bouncing them off of a contract

takeaways.what_they_do: They model work as 'a job is a contract plus a trigger' — cron or webhook (GitHub issue, PR, Slack) — which fires a multi-agent workflow that runs end-to-end to satisfy the contract, rather than a conversational loop.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a job is a contract plus a trigger

takeaways.technique: Start expensive/loose, then pin the 'how' from a golden trace
takeaways.what_they_do: Run a strong model to discover how to satisfy a loose contract, capture the trace, then 'shrink-wrap' it into a pinned procedural 'how' so cheaper models can execute it deterministically.

takeaways.technique: Cheap decision-model verifier at end of job
takeaways.what_they_do: They propose using fast, cheap 'system one'/decision models as a verifier that checks messy real-world state against the ideal contract (pass/fail), and as a semantic memoizer to detect when upstream state changed and re-trigger downstream work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: as a verifier on the end of the job like very very fast and cheap

takeaways.technique: Declarative contracts with pinned skills/tools and fail-if-missing deps
takeaways.what_they_do: Contracts declare sub-agents, specific skills and tools (e.g. force Exa over generic web search), and inputs/outputs; if required skills/CLIs aren't present the program refuses to compile/run.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you can't find those things, just don't run the program. Like we're not doing it the other way.

takeaways.technique: Composable intermediary contracts as checkpoints (DAG of contracts)
takeaways.what_they_do: Break a big workflow into a DAG of intermediary contracts; each step fulfills its contract and triggers the next, giving structure without hard-coding procedure.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can have intermediary steps that you almost think of them as like checkpoints... it hits this contract and fulfills this one, and then that causes the next one to keep going
